how-a-game-works: Stay out of the crease, its red edge included, and never go into the goalie.
In warm-ups and practice, never shoot at a goalie who isn't ready: facing you, set, with their stick down.
Say "our end" and "their end": the zones belong to your team, and teams swap ends between periods.
Keep your shifts short and go hard, and change when the puck is heading away from your net.
When the whistle goes, stop playing the puck and leave it for the official.
Offside: the puck must cross the blue line into their zone before you do, so keep your back skate dragging on the line until it has.
Avoid icing: carry the puck past the centre red line before sending it deep, and ask which line your league uses.
Keep your stick on the puck, not the other player; if you are beaten, move your feet instead of reaching.
gear-and-staying-safe: Wear your own helmet, never a second-hand one, with the chin strap done up every time; replace it after a serious knock.
Find out what your league requires, and wear a neck guard and a mouthguard every time you are on the ice.
Pads and skates should fit, not be big: check pads in your skating stance, and keep your skate edges sharp.
Keep your head up, meet the boards on an angle, and never turn your back to anyone coming at you, or duck.
Never put your stick or body into anyone's back: if you can see their numbers, pull up and play the puck.
If someone may have hurt their head or neck, don't move them except to keep their airway clear, leave their helmet on, and get help called.
A suspected concussion means off the ice for the day, and a medical professional before playing again, however fine you feel.
skating: Stay low, with your knees over your toes, and keep your eyes up, not just your chin.
Go into the boards on an angle, head up, and never turn your back to anyone coming at you, or duck.
Win races with short, quick first steps, pushing along the ice, and change speed on purpose: glide, then burst.
Train your outside edges, and cross over when you have room but turn tight when you don't.
Learn to stop on both sides, then go straight back the other way instead of looping.
Falling onto the ice, tuck your chin; sliding into the boards, keep your head up and meet them skates or side first.
If you might have a concussion, come off, tell someone, and stay off until a medical professional says you can play.
carrying-the-puck: Play with your head up, by building feel for the puck until your eyes can come up on their own.
Keep the puck on your far side, your body between it and the other player, low and wide, without pushing or grabbing.
Decide where the puck goes before you reach it: a pass, a rim hard along the boards, a reverse back the other way, or a chip.
On the boards, take contact along your side, head up, and never turn your back to anyone coming at you, or duck.
In your own end and through the middle, don't stickhandle: move the puck.
Look for a pass before you try a move; if you take a defender on, make them turn with one good fake.
When the puck arrives, keep striding: push it ahead and skate onto it rather than slowing down.
passing-and-catching: Move the puck, then move yourself to a new open spot.
Look over your shoulder while the pass is coming, and decide your next play before it lands.
Pass to where your teammate is going, on the side away from the other player.
Without the puck, get into a clear lane on time, show your blade flat on the ice, and call for it.
Cushion the puck with soft hands, and push your first touch into your next play.
Catch the puck with your body open to the ice, already facing your next play.
In your own end, never pass across the front of your goal, and ask your coach which other passes are allowed.
shooting: Shoot from the slot, the area right in front of the net, or pass to a teammate who is there.
In a game, shoot quickly from where you are, before the goalie is set, without stopping your feet.
Find a lane before you shoot: a shot that hits a shin pad is worse than no shot.
Make the goalie move first, then aim where they aren't; some coaches teach the corners instead, so ask yours.
Screen from just outside the crease, never touching the goalie, stick below everyone's shoulders, head up, and never duck.
Follow every shot to the net and shoot rebounds at once, playing the puck, never the goalie.
In warm-ups, keep shots off your goalie's head, and never shoot at the other team's goalie.
playing-without-the-puck: Notice the moment the puck changes hands and switch jobs at once; when your team wins it, go.
Be available, not just unmarked: blade flat on the ice, a clear lane to the puck, and a call.
Give the carrier two options at different angles: a triangle, not a line.
Skate to open space, not to the puck, and arrive late with speed; in your own end, get there now.
Drive the net hard, stop just outside the crease, and never go into the goalie.
On a loose puck, one player goes, one supports and someone stays back, so call who is going.
At the boards, arrive on an angle, head up; never turn your back to anyone coming at you, never duck, and never push or hit anyone in the back.
defending: Stay goal side, between your attacker and your net, and don't chase unless your team sends you.
Watch your attacker, not the puck; on the carrier, watch their chest and hips.
Keep your stick flat on the ice in the passing lane, never across a player.
Start skating backwards early and keep the gap, the space between you and the carrier, shrinking without lunging; ask your coach how tight.
Take the middle and steer the carrier toward the boards with your skating, never into the boards or their back.
When the puck is lost, sprint back to the inside of your attacker, and make sure somebody has the middle.
When the rush ends, find the front of your own net first.
playing-centre: In your own end, swing low so your defenceman has a safe pass, unless your coach wants you leaving early.
Keep the slot in front of your net filled: if you help in the corner, call a winger in behind you, unless you play man-on-man.
Under pressure, put the puck to the outside, and on the boards never turn your back to anyone coming at you, or duck.
Own the middle: carry through it head up, and coming back, take the late player trailing the carrier, on their inside.
In their end, shoot from the slot, screen the goalie, and go for rebounds, never into the goalie.
On the forecheck, chasing the puck in their end, arrive under control and steer the carrier, rather than running at them.
Take the faceoffs that matter seriously, and agree with your wingers where you will win the puck.
playing-wing: Going up the ice, stay wide in your lane, so one defender can't cover two of you.
Crash the net on every shot, head up, stopping just outside the crease and never going into the goalie.
With a good shot and a teammate at the net, lean toward shooting; pass if a teammate has an open side.
In your own end, stay high, level with their defenceman on your side; when your team wins the puck, come down the boards. Ask your coach.
On the boards, keep the puck on your far side, feet moving, and never turn your back to anyone coming at you, or duck.
When the other team gets the puck, sprint back, pick up the late player arriving behind the play, and never go into anyone's back.
playing-defence: Stay goal side, between the player you are covering and your net.
Work as a pair, one on the puck and one in front of your goal, unless your team plays man-on-man.
At your net, get inside first, then lift their stick low on the shaft, never at the hands; never shove or put your stick across anyone.
Never carry or pass the puck across the front of your own goal: go behind the net, or above the tops of the circles if your team does.
Going back for the puck, look over your shoulder, and never turn your back to anyone coming at you, or duck.
When you win it, look up the ice and move it early; if nothing is on, off the glass, never over it.
Win the gap, the space to the carrier, by skating backwards early and steering with your feet; never put your stick or body into anyone's back.
In their end, keep the puck in at the blue line, and only one of you goes low at a time.
playing-goal: Get on the line from the puck to the middle of your net: out, square and set as the shot leaves.
Choose your depth before the shot: out against a lone shooter, back when the puck is close or a pass is open.
Watch the puck all the way into your body, and move as soon as a pass leaves the stick.
Kill rebounds if you can; if you can't, steer them wide to the corners, never into the middle.
Stay on your feet until going down is the answer, and on a breakaway, be the last one to move.
Talk early, short and every time, using the call words your team has agreed.
Behind your net, keep it simple, and never pass the puck up the middle.
Have your own mask, even if you borrow the rest, and wear a neck guard.
After a hard shot off your mask, tell someone at the next stoppage; if you might be concussed, come off until a medical professional says you can play.
teamwork: Call "man on" early when someone is closing on the puck carrier, and say "time" only when you are sure.
Keep calls short, use names, be loud, and answer every call.
Be where your linemates expect you, and when a teammate leaves their spot to help, fill it, then get back to your own spot.
Keep giving a struggling teammate the puck, and never show frustration at them.
After a mistake, run your reset, a short routine to let it go, and name your next job before your next shift.
Say nothing to the referee, never get back at anyone, and stay out of any pushing and shoving.
Criticism of your play is coaching, but being put down as a person is not: tell someone at your club.
